question.passageWithMarkers: The structure of glass is, frankly, a bit of a mess. Clear and perfect as it might appear to our eyes, down at the molecular level, glass __(A) looks__ more like a random ball-pit of atoms. The technical term for this mess depends on __(B) who__ you're asking: for some scientists it is an "amorphous solid," for others a "supercooled liquid." In theory it's both liquid and solid, __(C) though__, given the way it behaves, in practice it's really the latter. In fact, at room temperature glass never behaves as a liquid, even an imperceptibly viscous one, even over long periods of time (though it can "sweat" if you don't add enough lime to the mix). Those misshapen sheets of glass you sometimes see in old stained-glass windows, thicker at the bottom than the top, __(D) is__ generally not that way because the glass is slowly sinking over time. Unless the church has endured temperatures of more than 400˚C, the chances are they are uneven because that's the way they were blown and solidified in the first place. Flat glass was only developed in the nineteenth century and we had to wait until the middle of the twentieth century for truly flat, thin sheets of glass. The paradox is that, __(E) despite__ it being one of the very oldest human-made substances, scientists still struggle to comprehend why glass behaves the way it does. Glass seems to obey most molecular laws. As one glassmaker put it, glass is not a material; it's a state.

question.passageWithMarkers: The structure of glass is, frankly, a bit of a mess. Clear and perfect as it might __(A) appear__ to our eyes, down at the molecular level, glass looks more like a random ball-pit of atoms. The technical term for this mess depends on who you're asking: for some scientists it is an "amorphous solid," for others a "supercooled liquid." In theory it's both liquid and solid, though, given the way it behaves, in practice it's really the latter. In fact, at room temperature glass never behaves as a liquid, even an imperceptibly viscous __(B) one__, even over long periods of time (though it can "sweat" if you don't add enough lime to the mix). Those __(C) misshapen__ sheets of glass you sometimes see in old stained-glass windows, thicker at the bottom than the top, are generally not that way because the glass is slowly sinking over time. Unless the church has endured temperatures of more than 400˚C, the chances are they are uneven because that's the way they were blown and solidified in the first place. Flat glass was only developed in the nineteenth century and we had to wait until the middle of the twentieth century for truly flat, thin sheets of glass. The paradox is that, __(D) despite__ it being one of the very oldest human-made substances, scientists still struggle to comprehend why glass behaves the way it does. Glass __(E) seem__ to obey most molecular laws. As one glassmaker put it, glass is not a material; it's a state.

question.passageWithMarkers: The structure of glass is, frankly, a bit of a mess. question.passageWithMarkers: In the pharmaceutical industry, algorithms are __(A) being employed__ to find treatments and drugs for rare diseases that to date haven't received much attention. The __(B) hard__ truth has always been that pharma devotes more research and development resources to diseases that affect the rich. The definition of rare has too often __(C) been associated__ with poor ― that is, even if a disease is quite prevalent in a population __(D) that__ cannot afford to pay for it (for example, people living in the developing world), the disease has been neglected compared to First World illnesses. By lowering the cost of data collection, mining, and analysis in drug development and clinical trials, AI can help offset imbalances in the pharmaceutical industry that __(E) directs__ attention to diseases that "pay," whether because the disease is more common or because it is prevalent among demographics that can pay more. We see the democratizing power of AI to broaden the attention of the medical and research communities to find cures to traditionally neglected health issues and among traditionally neglected populations.
